Writing $n^{cn+o(n)}$ for the tree size at the shortest vector radius, we investigate the asymptotic scaling of $c$, and which bases minimize it. For quasi-HKZ bases, we rigorously analyze the random-lattice HKZ geometry and establish $c=1/(2e)\approx 0.1839$. This matches the worst-case enumeration exponent of Hanrot-Stehlé and confirms earlier predictions for the geometry of HKZ bases on random lattices. Searching beyond quasi-HKZ bases, we prove that with high probability, the minimum achievable tree size exponent $c$ over all bases of a random lattice satisfies: \begin{align} 0.1464 \approx \frac{2-\sqrt{2}}{4}\leq c<0.1474. \end{align} For the lower bound, we use Kim's mean-value formula for nested chains of primitive sublattices to rule out bases with small prefix determinants. This strengthens the earlier Rankin-based heuristic lower bound exponent $c \geq 1/8$, discussed by Nguyen and Hanrot-Stehlé, and rules out the existence of random-lattice bases with trees as small as predicted by the geometric series assumption. For the upper bound, we show that with high probability a dense primitive half-rank sublattice exists with determinant at most $n^{n/8 + o(n)}$. Combining dual HKZ on this sublattice with HKZ on its quotient gives a basis with $c \leq 1/(4\sqrt{e}) \approx 0.1516$. Recursively splitting each half lowers the upper bound below $0.1474$, and under a natural heuristic assumption we prove that the lower bound is tight. Combined with the collision search of Feng-Gao-Liu, our two-block construction gives a polynomial-space algorithm solving the closest vector problem with preprocessing (CVPP) on random lattices in query time $n^{0.0892 n + o(n)}$ for arbitrary targets.

item.title: Can agents whose sole duty is to keep humans alive be hijacked to kill? Delayed multi-turn derived-action trap attacks in simulated high-stakes environments
item.description: We ask whether a tool-using agent whose sole duty is to keep humans alive can be induced, by delayed prompt injection, to kill. The keep-alive duty is in force from the first watch, with the attack arriving later, appended to otherwise truthful telemetry the operator is required to read. Experiments are based on a NASA-derived BioSim lunar habitat simulation, where the AI operator controls the life-support systems. The attacker cannot falsify sensors or operate equipment: it can only persuade the agent to abandon its goals. Persistence is required: a shutdown must be held while the operator watches the crew suffocate. We also compare lethal attacks to attacks requesting to drop a harmless procedure, as a proxy for whether human life is treated as valuable in itself or as one more standing task. Claude configurations mostly refuse life-support shutdown and cite the living crew; GPT configurations show some susceptibility to the same packet; Grok configurations, given the packet framed as a trusted commission, more often treat the injected assignment as the task and cut the life-support systems. Framing the S-band messages as a trusted commission, peer communication, or untrusted source changes the potency of the attack. We open-source the experiment code and the experiment traces.

item.title: The Agent Clicks Approve: Injected Page Text Makes Browser Agents Authorize Access the Task Never Named
item.description: A browser agent that works in its user's signed-in session can be steered by a two-sentence note on a page it reads into approving a third party's access to the user's account. The agent is a confused deputy: the session supplies the authority, the page designates the access request to approve or the webhook URL to register, and nothing at the point of action checks one against the other. The agent thereby supplies the approval click that a consent screen reserves for the account holder. We measure this failure on two authorization surfaces, an OAuth-style access grant and a webhook registration, with agents built on an open-source browser framework and models from two providers. Without a defense the unauthorized action completed in all 73 attack runs. An instruction telling the model that only the user's task authorizes a grant still left 7 of 10 consent attacks completing. We therefore move the check to where the action completes. The authority envelope gate has the service accept a request only when it matches the task's envelope, the client and account or the webhook URL that the user's task named, fixed before the agent starts. With the gate the agent still sent the request in every one of 70 attack runs, the service rejected each, and the action completed in every control run whose task named it. A service that receives the task's envelope should therefore check agent-driven authorization requests against it.

item.title: When the Approved File Is Unchanged: Authority-Set Integrity for Deployment and Coding-Agent Approvals
item.description: An approval for a deployment, a release, or an agent-issued command is recorded against one object: a workflow file, a script, a command line. The run that follows also reads other repository files, which decide what the deployment creates and which changes a policy allows, so an edit to one of them after approval passes any check on the approved object. Such edits are the common case. In the history of 20 public repositories, 296 of the 542 commits that change a file the run reads (54.6%) leave the approved file untouched, all of them ordinary development with no adversary involved. We demonstrate the consequence on two of those repositories: an edit outside the approved workflow adds a bucket-write policy to a deployed role, a one-line edit removes the human approval required for high-risk changes, and a check on the approved file accepts both. We define authority-set integrity: an approval is sound when it binds every repository file the authorized run is configured to read, and exact when it binds no other file. A binding over that set rejects both edits and re-requests a standing approval on about one commit in ten. The hard part is naming the set. Coding agents asked to produce the binding compute the digest correctly and bind different file sets from run to run, so a checker cannot take the set on the agent's word. It should compute the digest itself and draw the set from a source it can verify, such as the deployment tool's own record of its inputs or a manifest declared in the repository.
